prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level.
For the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with IceCube, opening neutrino astronomy.

statement.case_for: I keep my first-place discovery, IceCube, but after reading the ballots I no longer think it should carry a prize alone. Five colleagues ranked the optical lattice clock, four of them in their top three and three of them first, and I find their quantitative case persuasive: it is a measurement that nature answers back to, at the 1e-18 level, and it makes relativity, varying constants and dark-matter searches testable in the laboratory. That fits my conviction that physics needs clues from nature, not just ideas. IceCube supplies the complementary astrophysical half: a decade of independent evidence (diffuse flux, TXS 0506+056, Galactic plane) that a new observational window onto the universe exists. A two-part prize pairs a precision instrument achievement with a genuine discovery about the cosmos, which seems to me a balanced and defensible year, and both parts have the unusually clean property that the interpretation is stable and has been confirmed by other groups or analyses.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is mine: Halzen as a lone name for a collaboration-scale discovery. If the committee cannot defend that attribution against AMANDA and IceCube colleagues who built and analysed the detector, the B019 part collapses and the prize should fall back to B024 alone or B024 plus a different second part. For B024 the strongest reservation is lineage: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems may make it look incremental, and the instrument-versus-discovery question is real. Putting two parts together also means that each laureate's share is smaller, and I am not certain that the committee wants to split between atomic metrology and neutrino astronomy rather than keep a thematically unified prize.

responses.point: Olsson ranked IceCube only eighth and called the single-name configuration fragile, because the discovery belongs to a large collaboration and the longlist does not credit who else did the original work.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is the point where I have moved most since my opening. Where I differ is on how much weight it should carry: Halzen conceived AMANDA and IceCube and led the 2013 diffuse-flux discovery, and the Nobel tradition accepts that a spokesperson-founder can stand for a collaboration when the instrument is the achievement (as with LIGO). But I agree it is a vulnerability and that a prize is only credible if we can name Halzen with confidence, so I list it as an open uncertainty rather than claim it is resolved. I also notice that Eva's own ballot ranks the optical lattice clock third and the diffuse flux discovery as 'a genuine new window', which is why I think the pairing is not fanciful.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the lattice clock first as a textbook case of progress limited by measurement precision, with Katori's proposal and Ye's record performance giving a clean two-person prize, but he flagged the 2005 overlap and that the 1e-18 figures came from recollection.
responses.response: I agree with the two-person attribution and I like the experimentalist's framing: this is a result with numbers attached that others reproduce and surpass. I would qualify the 2005 worry. The comb gave the ruler; the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea that changed what the ruler can measure, so I do not think it is a second prize for the same discovery. What I would still want, as Secretary, is an outside expert report that checks the 1e-18 figures, the priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and whether the redefinition of the second is a prerequisite, rather than relying on any of our recollections, mine included.

responses.point: Pearce ranked the lattice clock first and IceCube second, calling IceCube squarely a major discovery, but noted that the 2015 oscillation prize may reduce the appetite for a second neutrino-mixing prize and that Halzen's single credit is difficult.
responses.response: As the chair, Mark sits between my two preferred parts, and I think his ballot is the best evidence that the pairing could draw broad support. On the 2015 point I would distinguish: 2015 was about oscillation (neutrino mass), while IceCube is about neutrinos as messengers from cosmic accelerators, so astrophysical neutrinos should not be penalised by it. The same argument is why I place theta-13 (B039) only as an alternative: it is a clean result but it does fall into the lineage that 2015 already recognised, which I judge as the more serious redundancy concern.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first, as the architecture underlying superconducting qubits, and the natural continuation of the 2025 circuit-tunnelling prize, while admitting Girvin's omission is a real allocation problem and flagging his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I respect the flag on proximity, and the physics case is strong, which is why I keep B042 as an alternative. My reservation is the one Göran himself raises: with four central names and a three-person limit, any configuration cuts into the theory-experiment core of the 2004 work, and it comes straight after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits. I would prefer not to hand the field a second prize so soon, and I think the committee should let more time pass before deciding between Girvin and Blais. I would be glad to be persuaded otherwise by someone closer to the field.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked 2D melting and the hexatic phase first as a simple, general mechanism with five decades of confirmation, which he says the 2016 prize left half-recognised.
responses.response: I find the mechanism elegant and I accept that recognition is late, but I do not think it should be preferred. It is the one that I as a sceptic of unconfirmed theory am least convinced about as a clean discovery, since Bernhard himself notes that simulations show first-order melting for hard disks, so the central claim is system-dependent. Overlap with Kosterlitz-Thouless in 2016 is a further problem. I would regard it as a real prize-worthy story only if the experimental evidence from colloids can be shown to carry the weight, and no one else on the committee ranked it.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen alone can be fairly credited for the IceCube discovery, or whether the committee must find additional names that the supplied credit does not contain (the three-person limit leaves room for two more).

Whether the 1e-18 performance of the lattice clocks and the priority of the magic-wavelength proposal hold up under an external expert report; several members, myself included, relied on recollection.
Whether the committee prefers a thematically unified single-achievement prize over a split between atomic metrology and neutrino astronomy.
Whether the origin of most of the IceCube diffuse flux, still unresolved, makes the discovery claim look premature to a majority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My supervisor David Gross and co-author Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any shortlisted candidate. As a co-opted member and Secretary my voting status is not documented, and I would flag that.
